terms.definition: Recovery Point Objective — the maximum amount of data loss (measured in time) a business can tolerate after a disaster. Controlled by backup frequency.
terms.example: If you back up every hour, your RPO is up to 60 minutes.

terms.definition: Recovery Time Objective — the maximum acceptable time a system can be down after a disaster before it must be restored and operational again.
terms.example: An RTO of 5 minutes means your system must be back online within 5 minutes of a failure.

terms.definition: Domain Name System — the internet's phone book that translates human-readable domain names (like amazon.com) into machine-readable IP addresses.
terms.example: When you type google.com, DNS resolves it to an IP like 142.250.64.46.

terms.definition: Amazon's fully managed DNS and traffic routing service, named after DNS port 53. Provides domain registration, DNS resolution, health checking, and traffic routing.
terms.example: Route 53 routes myapp.com traffic to the correct EC2 instance or CloudFront distribution.

terms.definition: A container in Route 53 for DNS records belonging to a specific domain. Can be public (internet-facing) or private (VPC-only).
terms.example: A public hosted zone for example.com contains A, CNAME, and MX records.

terms.definition: A Route 53 hosted zone that routes traffic from the internet to your resources. Accessible by anyone on the internet.
terms.example: Used when you want users worldwide to reach your website via DNS.

terms.definition: A Route 53 hosted zone that routes DNS traffic only within one or more associated VPCs — internal resources not exposed to the internet.
terms.example: Used to resolve internal service names like api.internal within a corporate VPC.

terms.definition: The middleman server (usually run by your ISP) that queries root name servers, TLD servers, and authoritative name servers to resolve a domain name on behalf of clients.
terms.example: When your browser queries google.com, your ISP's DNS resolver does the recursive lookup.

terms.definition: Time to Live — the duration (in seconds) for which a DNS resolver caches a DNS response before querying again. Lower TTL = faster change propagation.
terms.example: A TTL of 300 means resolvers cache the IP for 5 minutes before re-querying.

terms.definition: Route 53 routing policy that routes all traffic to a single resource. No health check support. Simplest policy.
terms.example: Point example.com to a single EC2 instance's IP address.

terms.definition: Route 53 policy that distributes traffic proportionally based on assigned weights. Supports health checks.
terms.example: Send 10% traffic to new app version (weight 10) and 90% to old version (weight 90).

terms.definition: Route 53 policy that routes traffic based on the geographic location of the DNS query origin (user's location).
terms.example: Route European users to EU servers, North American users to US servers.

terms.definition: Route 53 policy that routes users to the AWS Region with the lowest network latency for that user at that moment.
terms.example: A Singapore user gets routed to ap-southeast-1 if it has lower latency than us-east-1.

terms.definition: Route 53 policy that routes to a primary resource when healthy, and automatically switches to a secondary when the primary fails a health check. Active-passive DR pattern.
terms.example: Primary is us-east-1 EC2; secondary is eu-west-1 EC2. Health check triggers automatic failover.

terms.definition: Route 53 policy that returns up to 8 healthy IP addresses randomly per DNS query. Acts as a lightweight DNS-level load balancer.
terms.example: Three healthy servers return random IP selection per query; unhealthy servers are excluded.

terms.definition: Route 53 policy that routes traffic based on the CIDR IP address range of the client making the DNS query.
terms.example: Route traffic from 10.0.0.0/8 corporate network to internal servers, all others to public servers.

terms.definition: A Route 53 mechanism that monitors the health of endpoints (HTTP, HTTPS, TCP) and automatically excludes unhealthy ones from DNS responses.
terms.example: A health check on port 80 marks an EC2 unhealthy if it doesn't respond within the threshold.

terms.definition: A release strategy using two complete environments (Blue = current, Green = new). Traffic switches 100% instantly from Blue to Green. Rollback is instant.
terms.example: Switch Route 53 DNS from production EC2 fleet (Blue) to new-version fleet (Green).

terms.definition: A release strategy that gradually shifts a small percentage of traffic to a new version using weighted routing, testing with real users before full rollout.
terms.example: Send 5% traffic to new version, monitor error rates, increase to 20%, then 100%.

terms.definition: A DNS record type that maps a domain name to an IPv4 address. The most common DNS record type.
terms.example: example.com → 203.0.113.1

terms.definition: Canonical Name record — maps one domain name to another domain name (alias). Cannot be used for root domains (naked domains).
terms.example: www.example.com → example.com

terms.definition: Top-Level Domain name server — manages DNS delegation for a specific TLD (.com, .org, .io). Tells resolvers which authoritative name servers handle a domain.
terms.example: The .com TLD server directs queries for amazon.com to Route 53's name servers.

terms.definition: Amazon RDS configuration with a synchronous standby replica in a different Availability Zone. Provides automatic failover and near-zero RPO/RTO for relational databases.
terms.example: Primary RDS in us-east-1a fails → automatic promotion of standby in us-east-1b within 60–120 seconds.

terms.definition: Amazon Aurora feature that replicates data to a secondary AWS Region with RPO typically under 1 second and RTO under 1 minute.
terms.example: Primary in us-east-1, secondary read region in eu-west-1 for disaster recovery.

terms.definition: DynamoDB feature enabling multi-region, multi-active replication with near-zero RPO globally. All replicas accept reads and writes.
terms.example: Tables replicated across us-east-1, eu-west-1, and ap-southeast-1 with sub-second synchronisation.
